prompt.brief: Design a distributed tracing platform that propagates trace context across services, collects spans with low application overhead, samples intelligently, and supports fast latency and dependency analysis.
successSignals: Define trace and span identity, parentage, propagation, status, resource attributes, links, and clock-skew handling.
Buffer and batch spans at agents, apply head or tail sampling, cap high-cardinality attributes, and partition by trace ID.
Keep instrumentation non-blocking and preserve enough sampled evidence to diagnose tail latency and errors.
Explain partial traces, collector overload, late spans, retention, tenant privacy, indexing, and query cost.

functional: Propagate context, create spans, collect batches, sample traces, store searchable data, and query a trace or service dependency.
Show waterfall timing, errors, exemplars, service maps, latency percentiles, sampling decisions, and incomplete-span warnings.
Support tenant access, PII redaction, retention policies, trace deletion, collector health, and export to incident tools.
nonFunctional: Keep synchronous instrumentation overhead below 1% and target p95 query latency below 2 seconds for recent traces.
Ingest 10 billion spans per day with agent batching, sampling, compression, and trace-ID partitioning.
Make collector retries and batch ingestion deduplicable while distinguishing incomplete traces from healthy short traces.
Drop or sample low-value spans under pressure but preserve error, latency-tail, and policy-required traces.
scaleAssumptions: Collect 10 billion spans per day from 100,000 services with bursts during incidents.
Partition by tenant, trace ID, and event time; isolate high-cardinality services and incident surges.
Retain recent indexed spans and lower-cost raw archives under tenant-specific retention and privacy policy.

dataFlow.title: Accept Trace requests across distributed services
dataFlow.description: The Distributed tracing platform gateway authenticates the caller, validates the request, applies tenant policy and idempotency, then routes it to the owning service.

dataFlow.title: Commit the durable state
dataFlow.description: The ingestion path validates tenant policy and durably records the request context before acknowledging the client.

dataFlow.title: Publish the domain event
dataFlow.description: A durable outbox publishes committed Distributed tracing platform events; consumers deduplicate by event ID and track offsets.

dataFlow.title: Build the read model
dataFlow.description: Partitioned workers consume Distributed tracing platform events, update the serving projection, and expose lag or watermark metadata.

dataFlow.title: Serve and recover asynchronously
dataFlow.description: Serving reads use the Distributed tracing platform projection; replay, repair, export, and slow work remain off the request path.

architecture.title: Design a system to trace requests across microservices for debugging and performance monitoring. reference architecture
architecture.summary: The authoritative state records Trace requests across distributed services; asynchronous workers build serving projections while Trace ID and span ID propagation, Sampling strategies (head-based, tail-based), Time-series storage for spans stays isolated from the request path.

components.label: Distributed tracing platform state

components.label: Distributed tracing platform event backbone

components.label: Distributed tracing platform workers

components.label: Distributed tracing platform projection

components.label: Distributed tracing platform monitoring

connections.label: Validated Distributed tracing platform operation
connections.description: The gateway forwards a validated Distributed tracing platform operation after authentication, quota, and idempotency checks.

connections.label: Distributed tracing platform state commit

connections.label: Distributed tracing platform event

connections.description: Workers assemble traces, apply tail-sampling decisions, build indexes, and archive raw spans.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Distributed tracing platform commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Distributed tracing platform writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Distributed tracing platform version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Distributed tracing platform by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Distributed tracing platform work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Distributed tracing platform projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Distributed tracing platform projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Distributed tracing platform records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Distributed tracing platform latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.

rubric.description: The answer defines propagation, ingestion, sampling, indexing, query behavior, scale, privacy, and recovery.
Entities and keys cover tenants, traces, spans, batches, sampling policies, indexes, and retention state.
Partitioning, cache behavior, queues, backpressure, and hot-key handling are explicit.
Idempotency, replay, recovery, degraded reads, and observability protect committed state.
The candidate can explain Distributed tracing platform consistency, push/pull, managed services, and the scale boundary.
